decks.title: Biodiversity and Conservation — Part 1: Biodiversity, its patterns and importance
goals: Describe genetic, species and ecological diversity with examples
Estimate global and Indian species numbers
Explain latitudinal gradients and the species–area relationship
Explain why species diversity matters to ecosystems

slides.heading: Biodiversity and Conservation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the variety of life, how it is distributed, and why it matters.

visual.alt: Flow of three levels of biodiversity

slides.narration: Biodiversity is the term popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson to describe the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation. The most important levels are genetic diversity, species diversity and ecological diversity.

slides.heading: Three levels of diversity
slides.body_md: Diversity exists within species, among species and among ecosystems.

rows: Rauwolfia vomitoria in different Himalayan ranges varies in the potency and concentration of reserpine; India has more than 50,000 strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango
The Western Ghats have a greater diversity of amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats
India’s deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows give greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country such as Norway

visual.alt: Table of the three levels of biodiversity with Indian examples

slides.narration: A single medicinal plant can differ in its active chemical from one mountain range to another; that is genetic diversity. Different regions hold different numbers of species. And a country with deserts, forests, mangroves and reefs has far more ecological diversity than one with only a few kinds of ecosystem.

slides.heading: How many species?
slides.body_md: The IUCN (2004) put the number of described plant and animal species at slightly **more than 1.5 million**. **Robert May** estimated the global total at about **7 million**. More than **70 percent** of recorded species are **animals**; plants make up no more than **22 percent**. Among animals, **insects** are the most species-rich group.

slides.narration: We know only a fraction of the species on Earth, especially among insects and microbes. Out of every ten animals, seven are insects. The number of fungal species alone is more than the combined total of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: India’s share
slides.body_md: India has only 2.4 percent of the world’s land area but 8.1 percent of global species diversity. How many times its land share is its share of species?
bullets: Ratio $= \dfrac{8.1}{2.4} \approx 3.4$.
India is one of the **12 mega diversity countries** of the world; nearly **45,000 plant species** and twice as many animal species have been recorded.
Applying May’s estimates, more than 1,00,000 plant and 3,00,000 animal species may still await discovery in India.

visual.alt: Worked table: India’s species share is about 3.4 times its land share

slides.narration: Divide eight point one by two point four to get about three point four. India holds more than three times as large a share of the world’s species as of its land, which is why it is counted among the mega diversity countries.

slides.narration: Quick check. Is this variation within one species or among species?

slides.body_md: Diversity generally **decreases from the equator towards the poles**. The tropics (23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas.

slides.narration: Colombia, near the equator, has about fourteen hundred species of birds, while Greenland, far to the north, has only fifty-six. A tropical forest in Ecuador can have up to ten times as many species of vascular plants as a temperate forest of the same area. The Amazon rain forest has the greatest biodiversity on Earth.

slides.heading: Why are the tropics so rich?
slides.body_md: Ecologists and evolutionary biologists have proposed several hypotheses.

rows: Temperate regions were subjected to frequent glaciations; tropical latitudes remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years, giving a long evolutionary time for diversification
Tropical environments are less seasonal, more constant and predictable, promoting niche specialisation
More solar energy in the tropics contributes to higher productivity, which might contribute indirectly to greater diversity

visual.alt: Table of three explanations of greater tropical diversity

slides.narration: Speciation takes time, and the tropics have had a long undisturbed history. Their steady, predictable climate allows species to specialise in narrow niches. And abundant sunlight drives high productivity, which can support more kinds of organisms.

slides.heading: Species–area relationship
slides.body_md: **Alexander von Humboldt** observed that within a region, species richness **increases with explored area, but only up to a limit**. On a logarithmic scale the relationship is a **straight line**.

visual.alt: Species–area curve on ordinary axes and straight lines on log–log axes with slopes Z for regions and continents

slides.narration: S is species richness, A is area, C is the Y-intercept and Z is the slope, also called the regression coefficient. For most regions and groups Z lies between about zero point one and zero point two. For very large areas such as whole continents the slope is much steeper, about zero point six to one point two.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: finding Z
slides.body_md: A survey finds 40 plant species in 10 square kilometres and 80 species in 1000 square kilometres of the same region. Estimate Z. By what factor would species rise if the area grew tenfold with Z = 0.15?
bullets: $Z = \dfrac{\log 80 - \log 40}{\log 1000 - \log 10} = \dfrac{\log 2}{2} \approx 0.15$.
Tenfold area: species rise by $10^{0.15} \approx 1.41$ times.
Both values are typical of a region, not a continent.

visual.alt: Worked table: Z about 0.15

slides.narration: A hundredfold increase in area only doubled the species, so the slope on log axes is small, about zero point one five. With such a slope, ten times the area gives only about one point four times as many species.

slides.heading: Why does species diversity matter?
slides.body_md: A **stable** community should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year, must be resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances, and must resist invasions by alien species.

rows: Plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass, and higher diversity raised productivity
An ecosystem is like an aeroplane held by rivets (species); losing a few may not matter at first, but losing key rivets, or many, endangers the whole

visual.alt: Table of evidence and ideas on why species diversity matters

slides.narration: Removing rivets from the seats may not matter, but removing rivets from the wings, the key species that drive major ecosystem functions, is serious. Rich biodiversity is essential for ecosystem health and for the survival of the human race.

slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about tropical diversity.

slides.body_md: What is the usual range of Z for species–area relationships within a region?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Levels: genetic (Rauwolfia, rice, mango), species (Western Ghats amphibians), ecological (India vs Norway).
Over 1.5 million species described; May’s estimate about 7 million; animals over 70 percent, insects over 70 percent of animals.
India: 2.4 percent of land, 8.1 percent of species; one of 12 mega diversity countries.
Diversity decreases from equator to poles: time, stable climate, more solar energy.
Species–area: log S = log C + Z log A; Z 0.1–0.2 (regions), 0.6–1.2 (continents).
Diversity brings stability and productivity (Tilman); rivet popper hypothesis (Ehrlich).

rows: More species in larger areas, up to a limit

visual.alt: Summary table of two patterns of biodiversity

slides.narration: To recap: biodiversity exists at genetic, species and ecological levels. It is richest in the tropics and rises with area. And diverse communities are more stable and productive, as Tilman’s experiments showed.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **one Indian example** for each level of diversity.
Write the **species–area equation** and the **Z ranges**.
Give **three reasons** for tropical richness.
Explain the **rivet popper hypothesis** in your own words.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give an Indian example for each level of diversity. Write the species–area equation and the ranges of Z. Learn three reasons for tropical richness. And explain the rivet popper idea simply.

decks.title: Biodiversity and Conservation — Part 2: Loss of biodiversity
goals: Describe the scale of recent extinctions
Explain the effects of biodiversity loss
Explain the four major causes ("evil quartet") with examples

slides.heading: Loss of biodiversity
slides.body_md: Part 2 — species are disappearing far faster than in pre-human times, mainly because of human activities.

visual.alt: Flow from human activities through four causes to species loss and weaker ecosystems

slides.narration: The colonisation of tropical Pacific islands by humans is said to have led to the extinction of more than two thousand species of native birds. The IUCN Red List of two thousand and four documents the extinction of seven hundred and eighty-four species in the last five hundred years.

slides.heading: Recent extinctions
slides.body_md: The IUCN Red List (2004) documents **784 extinctions** in the last 500 years: **338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants**. In the last twenty years alone, **27 species** have disappeared.

rows: Three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan, Caspian)

visual.alt: Table of recent extinctions with places

slides.narration: Careful analysis shows that the extinctions are not random; some groups, like amphibians, appear more vulnerable. More than fifteen thousand five hundred species worldwide face the threat of extinction.

slides.heading: The sixth extinction
slides.body_md: Earth has seen five episodes of mass extinction since life originated. The **sixth extinction**, now in progress, differs: current species extinction rates are estimated to be **100 to 1,000 times faster** than in pre-human times, and **human activities** are responsible.

visual.alt: Table of the share of species in four groups that face the threat of extinction

slides.narration: Ecologists warn that if the present trends continue, nearly half of all species on Earth might be wiped out within the next hundred years. Amphibians are among the hardest hit.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading extinction data
slides.body_md: Of the 784 documented extinctions, 338 were vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants. What percentage were plants, and which group lost most species?
bullets: Plants $= \dfrac{87}{784} \times 100 \approx 11.1$ percent.
Invertebrates lost the most species (359).

visual.alt: Worked table: plants 11.1 percent of extinctions

slides.narration: First confirm the three groups add to seven hundred and eighty-four. Plants are about eleven percent of the documented extinctions, and invertebrates form the largest group, though many invertebrate extinctions probably go unrecorded.

slides.heading: Effects of biodiversity loss
slides.body_md: Loss of biodiversity in a region may lead to:

rows: For example, less able to withstand drought
Plant productivity, water use, and pest and disease cycles fluctuate more

visual.alt: Table of three effects of biodiversity loss

slides.narration: Fewer species means a less productive and less stable ecosystem. It copes less well with drought, and processes such as water use and pest outbreaks become more unpredictable.

slides.heading: Quick check: rate of extinction
slides.body_md: How much faster are current extinction rates estimated to be than in pre-human times?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the range given for the sixth extinction.

slides.heading: The evil quartet: habitat loss and over-exploitation
slides.body_md: **Habitat loss and fragmentation** is the most important cause. **Over-exploitation** has driven several species to extinction.

rows: Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 percent of Earth’s land surface, now no more than 6 percent; the Amazon, the “lungs of the planet”, is cleared for soya beans and cattle pasture
Mammals and birds needing large territories, and migratory animals, are badly affected
Steller’s sea cow and the passenger pigeon became extinct; many marine fish populations are over-harvested

visual.alt: Table of habitat loss, fragmentation and over-exploitation with examples

slides.narration: When large habitats are broken into small fragments, animals that need large territories or migrate decline. And when need turns to greed, harvesting outpaces reproduction, as it did for Steller’s sea cow and the passenger pigeon.

slides.heading: Quick check: fragmentation
slides.body_md: Which animals suffer most when a large forest is split into small patches?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of animals that need a lot of space or travel far.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: shrinking rain forests
slides.body_md: Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 percent of the Earth’s land surface but now cover no more than 6 percent. What fraction of the original rain-forest area has been lost?
bullets: Lost $= \dfrac{14 - 6}{14} \times 100 \approx 57.1$ percent.
More than half of the original rain-forest cover has gone.
Habitat loss is the most important cause of extinctions of plants and animals.

visual.alt: Worked table: about 57.1 percent of rain forest lost

slides.narration: A fall from fourteen to six percent of the land surface means eight out of fourteen parts are gone, about fifty-seven percent of the original forest. Since rain forests hold so many species, this loss is especially serious.

slides.heading: The evil quartet: alien invasions and co-extinctions
slides.body_md: **Alien species invasions:** some introduced species become invasive and cause decline or extinction of indigenous species. **Co-extinctions:** when a species becomes extinct, species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct.

rows: Nile perch in Lake Victoria (East Africa) led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish; carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia); illegally introduced African catfish Clarias gariepinus threatens native catfishes
When a host fish becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites also becomes extinct; a plant and its pollinator in a co-evolved mutualism

visual.alt: Table of alien species invasions and co-extinctions with examples

slides.narration: An alien predator or competitor, free of its natural enemies, can wipe out native species, as the Nile perch did to cichlid fishes. And because many species depend on each other, the loss of one, such as a host or a pollinator, can drag others down with it.

slides.heading: Quick check: alien species
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the Nile perch.
slides.narration: Quick check. Was the perch native to Lake Victoria?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: IUCN (2004): 784 extinctions in 500 years (338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates, 87 plants); dodo, quagga, thylacine, Steller’s sea cow, three tiger subspecies.
Sixth extinction: 100–1,000 times faster than pre-human rates; caused by humans.
Threatened: 12 percent birds, 23 percent mammals, 32 percent amphibians, 31 percent gymnosperms.
Effects: lower production, lower resistance to drought, more variable processes.
Evil quartet: habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions, co-extinctions.

visual.alt: Summary table of the evil quartet with examples

slides.narration: To recap: extinctions are now running far faster than ever before, and people are the cause. The four main drivers are habitat loss, over-exploitation, alien species and co-extinctions.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the **evil quartet** with one **example** each.
Explain **why fragmentation** harms large and migratory animals.
Give **three effects** of biodiversity loss.
Know a few **recent extinctions** with their places.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Name the four causes with an example each. Explain fragmentation. Give three effects of biodiversity loss. And remember a few recent extinctions with where they happened.

decks.title: Biodiversity and Conservation — Part 3: Conservation
goals: Give the narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical reasons for conservation
Compare in situ and ex situ conservation with examples
Explain hotspots, protected areas, sacred groves, Ramsar sites and the Red Data Book

slides.heading: Biodiversity conservation
slides.body_md: Part 3 — why we should conserve biodiversity, and how.

visual.alt: Flow from reasons for conservation to in situ, ex situ and global action

slides.narration: The reasons for conserving biodiversity can be grouped into three categories: narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical. Conservation itself can happen in the species’ natural home or away from it.

slides.heading: Why conserve biodiversity?
slides.body_md: Three kinds of argument.

rows: Food, firewood, fibre, construction material, tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes; more than 25 percent of drugs sold today come from plants; 25,000 plant species are used in traditional medicine; bioprospecting for useful products
Ecosystem services: the Amazon forest produces about 20 percent of the oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere through photosynthesis; pollination by bees, bumblebees, birds and bats; aesthetic pleasure
Every species has an intrinsic value, even if not of economic value; we have a moral duty to pass our biological legacy to future generations

visual.alt: Table of three arguments for conserving biodiversity

slides.narration: Nature gives us food, medicines and raw materials directly. It also provides services we could hardly pay for, such as oxygen and pollination. And beyond usefulness, every species has a right to exist and a value of its own.

slides.heading: Quick check: arguments
slides.body_md: Pollination of crops by bees is an example of which argument for conservation?
slides.narration: Quick check. Is this a direct product or a service?

slides.heading: In situ conservation: hotspots
slides.body_md: When we conserve and protect a whole ecosystem, its biodiversity at all levels is protected. **Biodiversity hotspots** are regions with **very high species richness** and a **high degree of endemism** (species found nowhere else).

rows: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka; Indo-Burma; Himalaya
Together less than 2 percent of Earth’s land area
Strict protection could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 percent

visual.alt: Table of facts about biodiversity hotspots

slides.narration: Conservationists cannot protect everything at once, so they focus on hotspots, small areas packed with species that live nowhere else. Three of the world’s thirty-four hotspots cover India’s exceptionally rich regions.

slides.heading: Protected areas and sacred groves
slides.body_md: In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as **biosphere reserves**, **national parks** and **wildlife sanctuaries**. India also has a history of **religious and cultural traditions** that protect nature.

visual.alt: Table of sacred grove regions in India

slides.narration: In many cultures, tracts of forest were set aside and all trees and wildlife within them were venerated and given total protection. In Meghalaya, sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants.

slides.heading: Ramsar sites and the Red Data Book
slides.body_md: **Ramsar sites** are wetlands of international importance listed under the **Ramsar Convention** (signed at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971) for conservation and wise use. The **Red Data Book**, or Red List, maintained by the **IUCN**, documents species threatened with extinction.

rows: Protects an internationally important wetland and its biodiversity
Records the conservation status of species, such as critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable
Biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries conserve habitats in situ

visual.alt: Table of conservation tools and their purposes

slides.narration: Wetlands are among the most productive and threatened habitats, so the Ramsar Convention lists important ones for protection. The Red Data Book tells us which species are most at risk, so that conservation efforts can be directed where they are most needed.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: in situ or ex situ?
slides.body_md: Classify each conservation action and give a reason.
bullets: Declaring a forest as a national park to protect tigers → **in situ**: protected in its natural habitat.
Storing seeds of rice varieties in a seed bank → **ex situ**: kept away from the natural habitat.
Protecting a sacred grove in Meghalaya → **in situ**.
Breeding an endangered deer in a zoo and keeping its gametes in cryopreservation → **ex situ**.

visual.alt: Worked table classifying four actions as in situ or ex situ

slides.narration: Ask one question: is the organism protected where it naturally lives? If yes, it is in situ conservation. If it is taken out and kept in a zoo, garden, seed bank or frozen store, it is ex situ.

slides.heading: Quick check: hotspots
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about biodiversity hotspots.
slides.narration: Quick check. What two features define a hotspot?

slides.heading: Ex situ conservation
slides.body_md: Threatened animals and plants are taken out of their natural habitat and placed in special settings where they can be protected and given special care.

rows: Zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks
Protect and breed threatened species; some animals extinct in the wild survive only in zoos
Gametes of threatened species kept viable and fertile for long periods
Seeds of commercially important plants stored for long periods

visual.alt: Table of ex situ conservation methods and uses

slides.narration: Ex situ methods are a safety net. When a species has almost vanished from the wild, zoos and seed banks can keep it alive. Modern techniques let us freeze gametes, fertilise eggs in the laboratory and multiply plants from small pieces of tissue.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning conservation
slides.body_md: A rare orchid grows only in one sacred grove and is pollinated by a single bee species. Suggest a conservation plan that uses both approaches.
bullets: **In situ:** protect the whole grove, so that the orchid **and its pollinator** survive together (avoiding co-extinction).
**Ex situ:** store seeds in a **seed bank** and grow plants by **tissue culture** in a botanical garden as a backup.
Check its status in the **Red Data Book** and record it, so it gets priority.

nodes.label: Seed bank and tissue culture (ex situ)

visual.alt: Worked flow of an in situ and ex situ plan for a rare orchid

slides.narration: In situ protection keeps the orchid in its habitat together with the bee it depends on, so neither is lost. Ex situ seed banks and tissue culture provide a backup in case the wild population fails.

slides.heading: Global commitments
slides.body_md: Biodiversity knows no political boundaries, so conservation is a collective responsibility of all nations.

rows: All nations called on to take measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable use of its benefits
World Summit on Sustainable Development, Johannesburg, 2002
190 countries pledged to achieve, by 2010, a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss

visual.alt: Table of two international meetings on biodiversity

slides.narration: The historic convention on biological diversity at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro called on all nations to conserve biodiversity. Ten years later, at Johannesburg, one hundred and ninety countries pledged to slow the rate of biodiversity loss.

slides.heading: Quick check: ex situ
slides.body_md: Which of these is an ex situ method of conservation?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which method keeps material away from the natural habitat?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Reasons: narrowly utilitarian (products, drugs, bioprospecting), broadly utilitarian (oxygen, pollination, aesthetics), ethical (intrinsic value).
In situ: hotspots (34; three cover India; under 2 percent of land), biosphere reserves, national parks, sanctuaries, sacred groves, Ramsar wetlands.
Red Data Book (IUCN) records threatened species.
Ex situ: zoos, botanical gardens, safari parks, cryopreservation, in vitro fertilisation, tissue culture, seed banks.
Rio (1992) and Johannesburg (2002) summits.

visual.alt: Summary table of in situ and ex situ approaches

slides.narration: To recap: we conserve biodiversity for its products, its services and its own sake. In situ conservation protects whole habitats, while ex situ methods keep threatened species safe elsewhere. And nations have pledged to work together.

sections.heading: 1. Biodiversity and its levels
sections.body_md:
**Biodiversity**, a term popularised by the sociobiologist **Edward Wilson**, is the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation.

- **Genetic diversity:** a single species may show high diversity at the genetic level over its range. *Rauwolfia vomitoria* growing in different Himalayan ranges varies in the potency and concentration of the chemical **reserpine**. India has more than **50,000** genetically different strains of rice and **1,000** varieties of mango.
- **Species diversity:** diversity at the species level; the **Western Ghats** have a greater amphibian species diversity than the **Eastern Ghats**.
- **Ecological diversity:** diversity of ecosystems; India, with its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, has greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway.

**How many species?** According to the IUCN (2004), slightly more than **1.5 million** plant and animal species have been described. **Robert May** placed the global estimate at about **7 million**. More than **70 percent** of all recorded species are **animals**; plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) make up no more than **22 percent**. Among animals, **insects** are the most species-rich group, making up more than 70 percent of the total; out of every 10 animals, 7 are insects. The number of fungal species exceeds the combined total of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.

**India** has only **2.4 percent** of the world’s land area but **8.1 percent** of global species diversity, making it one of the **12 mega diversity countries**. Nearly **45,000** species of plants and twice as many animals have been recorded; applying May’s estimates, more than 1,00,000 plant and 3,00,000 animal species may yet be discovered.

sections.heading: 2. Patterns of biodiversity and its importance
sections.body_md:
**Latitudinal gradients.** Species diversity generally **decreases from the equator towards the poles**. The tropics (23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas. Colombia, near the equator, has nearly **1,400** species of birds; New York at 41° N has **105**; Greenland at 71° N has **56**. India, with much of its land in tropical latitudes, has more than **1,200** bird species. A forest in a tropical region like Ecuador has up to **10 times** as many species of vascular plants as a forest of equal area in a temperate region like the Midwest of the USA. The **Amazon** rain forest has the greatest biodiversity on Earth.

Why the tropics are richer:
1. Speciation is generally a function of **time**. Temperate regions were subjected to frequent **glaciations** in the past, whereas tropical latitudes remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years.
2. Tropical environments are **less seasonal**, more constant and predictable, which promotes **niche specialisation**.
3. More **solar energy** is available in the tropics, contributing to higher **productivity**, which might in turn contribute indirectly to greater diversity.

**Species–area relationship.** **Alexander von Humboldt** observed that within a region species richness increases with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit. The relation is a rectangular hyperbola, and on a logarithmic scale a straight line: $\log S = \log C + Z \log A$, where S is species richness, A area, C the Y-intercept and Z the slope (regression coefficient). Z lies in the range **0.1 to 0.2** regardless of taxonomic group or region; for very large areas such as entire continents the slope is much steeper, with Z of **0.6 to 1.2** (for example, frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents, slope 1.15).

**Importance of species diversity.** A stable community does not show too much variation in productivity from year to year, is resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances, and resists invasion by alien species. **David Tilman**’s long-term outdoor plot experiments showed that plots with more species had less year-to-year variation in total biomass, and that greater diversity contributed to higher productivity. **Paul Ehrlich**’s **rivet popper hypothesis** compares an ecosystem to an aeroplane whose rivets are species: losing a few rivets may not affect flight at first, but as more are removed the plane becomes dangerously weak, and losing rivets on the wings (key species that drive major ecosystem functions) is more serious than losing those on the seats.

sections.heading: 3. Loss of biodiversity
sections.body_md:
The colonisation of tropical Pacific islands by humans is said to have led to the extinction of more than 2,000 species of native birds. The **IUCN Red List (2004)** documents the extinction of **784 species** (338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years. Recent extinctions include the **dodo** (Mauritius), **quagga** (Africa), **thylacine** (Australia), **Steller’s sea cow** (Russia) and three subspecies of tiger (**Bali, Javan, Caspian**). In the last twenty years alone, 27 species have disappeared. More than **15,500** species worldwide face the threat of extinction; at present **12 percent** of bird species, **23 percent** of mammal species, **32 percent** of amphibian species and **31 percent** of gymnosperm species face this threat.

The **sixth extinction**, now in progress, differs from the five earlier mass extinctions: current rates are estimated to be **100 to 1,000 times faster** than in pre-human times, and **human activities** are responsible. If present trends continue, nearly half of all species might be wiped out within the next 100 years.

**Effects** of loss of biodiversity in a region: a decline in plant production; lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought; and increased variability in certain ecosystem processes such as plant productivity, water use, and pest and disease cycles.

**Causes — the “evil quartet”:**
1. **Habitat loss and fragmentation** — the most important cause. Tropical rain forests once covered more than **14 percent** of the Earth’s land surface and now cover no more than **6 percent**. The **Amazon** rain forest, called the “lungs of the planet”, is being cut and cleared for cultivating soya beans or for conversion to grassland for raising beef cattle. When large habitats are broken into fragments, mammals and birds needing large territories and animals with migratory habits are badly affected.
2. **Over-exploitation** — when need turns to greed. **Steller’s sea cow** and the **passenger pigeon** became extinct through over-exploitation; many marine fish populations are over-harvested.
3. **Alien species invasions** — the **Nile perch** introduced into **Lake Victoria** in East Africa eventually led to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than **200 species of cichlid fish**. Invasive weeds such as **carrot grass (Parthenium)**, **Lantana** and **water hyacinth (Eichhornia)** damage the environment; the illegal introduction of the African catfish ***Clarias gariepinus*** for aquaculture threatens indigenous catfishes in Indian rivers.
4. **Co-extinctions** — when a species becomes extinct, plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct, e.g. the unique parasites of an extinct host fish, or a co-evolved plant and its pollinator.

sections.heading: 4. Biodiversity conservation
sections.body_md:
**Why conserve?**
- **Narrowly utilitarian:** humans derive countless direct economic benefits — food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, and industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes). More than **25 percent** of the drugs currently sold in the market are derived from plants, and **25,000** plant species contribute to traditional medicines used by native peoples. Nations rich in biodiversity can expect benefits from **bioprospecting** (exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance).
- **Broadly utilitarian:** biodiversity provides **ecosystem services**. The **Amazon** forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, about **20 percent** of the total oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere. **Pollination** by bees, bumblebees, birds and bats is another service, as are the aesthetic pleasures of nature.
- **Ethical:** every species has an **intrinsic value**, even if not of current economic value to us; we have a moral duty to care for their well-being and to pass on our biological legacy in good order to future generations.

**In situ (on site) conservation** protects a whole ecosystem and hence its biodiversity at all levels.
- **Biodiversity hotspots** are regions with **very high levels of species richness** and a **high degree of endemism**. Initially 25 were identified, and 9 more were added, giving **34**. Three cover India’s exceptionally rich regions: **Western Ghats and Sri Lanka**, **Indo-Burma** and **Himalaya**. Hotspots together cover less than **2 percent** of the Earth’s land area, yet harbour a very high number of species; strict protection could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost **30 percent**.
- In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as **biosphere reserves**, **national parks** and **wildlife sanctuaries**. (The textbook gives counts of 14, 90 and 448; official current counts are higher.)
- **Sacred groves:** tracts of forest set aside, with all trees and wildlife venerated and protected — in the **Khasi and Jaintia Hills** (Meghalaya), the **Aravalli Hills** (Rajasthan), the **Western Ghat** regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the **Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar** areas of Madhya Pradesh. In Meghalaya they are the last refuges for many rare and threatened plants.
- **Ramsar sites:** wetlands of international importance designated under the **Ramsar Convention** (Ramsar, Iran, 1971) for conservation and wise use.
- **Red Data Book:** the IUCN Red List records the conservation status of species (for example critically endangered, endangered, vulnerable), guiding conservation priorities.

**Ex situ (off site) conservation:** threatened animals and plants are taken out of their natural habitat and protected in **zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks**; many animals extinct in the wild are maintained in zoos. **Cryopreservation** keeps gametes viable and fertile for long periods; eggs can be fertilised **in vitro**; plants can be propagated by **tissue culture**; seeds of commercially important plants are stored in **seed banks**.

**International efforts:** the **Earth Summit** at **Rio de Janeiro (1992)** called on all nations to take measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable use of its benefits; at the **World Summit on Sustainable Development** in **Johannesburg (2002)**, **190 countries** pledged to achieve, by 2010, a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Defining a hotspot by species richness alone (endemism is also needed).
- Calling seed banks or zoos in situ conservation.
- Saying diversity increases towards the poles.
- Giving Z for continents as 0.1–0.2 (that is for regions; continents 0.6–1.2).
- Listing climate change or pollution as members of the evil quartet (the four are habitat loss, over-exploitation, alien species and co-extinctions).
- Mixing up narrowly and broadly utilitarian arguments.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: name a level, a cause, a hotspot, an extinct species or a method.
- 2–3-mark answers: three levels with examples; reasons for tropical richness; species–area relation; three arguments for conservation.
- 5-mark answers: the evil quartet with examples; in situ and ex situ conservation; patterns of biodiversity.
- Case-based items: species–area data, extinction data, invasive species or conservation planning, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: Describe the latitudinal gradient in species diversity and the species–area relationship, and explain why species diversity matters to an ecosystem.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Latitudinal gradient.** Species diversity generally decreases from the equator towards the poles. Colombia, near the equator, has nearly 1,400 bird species, New York at 41° N has 105 and Greenland at 71° N has only 56. A tropical forest in Ecuador may have up to ten times as many vascular plant species as an equal temperate forest. Explanations are the long undisturbed evolutionary time of the tropics, which escaped the glaciations of temperate regions; their less seasonal, more predictable environment, which favours niche specialisation; and their greater solar energy and productivity.

**Species–area relationship.** Alexander von Humboldt observed that species richness increases with explored area, up to a limit. On logarithmic axes the relation is a straight line, log S = log C + Z log A, where Z, the slope, is about 0.1–0.2 within regions and 0.6–1.2 for very large areas such as continents.

**Importance.** David Tilman’s experiments showed that plots with more species varied less in biomass from year to year and were more productive. A diverse community is more stable, more resistant or resilient to disturbance and harder for alien species to invade. Ehrlich’s rivet popper hypothesis warns that losing key species can make the whole ecosystem fail.

questions.solution_md: Gradient with reasons; species–area; importance.

questions.stem_md: What is biodiversity? Describe its three levels with examples, and summarise how many species are known globally and in India.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Biodiversity**, a term popularised by Edward Wilson, is the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation.

**Genetic diversity** is variation within a species: Rauwolfia vomitoria in different Himalayan ranges varies in the potency and concentration of reserpine, and India has more than 50,000 strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango. **Species diversity** is the variety of species: the Western Ghats have more amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats. **Ecological diversity** is the variety of ecosystems: India, with deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, has more than a country such as Norway.

**Global numbers.** The IUCN (2004) lists slightly more than 1.5 million described species, while Robert May estimated about 7 million in all. More than 70 percent of recorded species are animals and no more than 22 percent plants; insects make up more than 70 percent of animals.

**India.** With only 2.4 percent of the world’s land, India has 8.1 percent of its species and is one of 12 mega diversity countries. About 45,000 plant species and twice as many animal species are recorded, and many more remain to be discovered.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the sixth extinction? Describe the four major causes of biodiversity loss, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Sixth extinction.** Earth has seen five mass extinctions. The sixth, now in progress, differs because current rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times, and human activities are responsible. The IUCN Red List (2004) documents 784 extinctions in 500 years, including the dodo, quagga, thylacine, Steller’s sea cow and three subspecies of tiger.

**Habitat loss and fragmentation** is the most important cause. Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 percent of the land surface and now cover no more than 6 percent; the Amazon is cleared for soya beans and cattle. Fragmentation badly affects animals needing large territories and migratory species.

**Over-exploitation** occurs when need turns to greed: Steller’s sea cow and the passenger pigeon were hunted to extinction, and many marine fish are over-harvested.

**Alien species invasions:** the Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria wiped out more than 200 cichlid species; Parthenium, Lantana and water hyacinth damage Indian ecosystems; the African catfish Clarias gariepinus threatens native catfishes.

**Co-extinctions:** when a species becomes extinct, those associated with it obligatorily also disappear, such as the parasites of an extinct host fish or a co-evolved plant and pollinator.

questions.stem_md: Compare in situ and ex situ conservation of biodiversity, describing the methods used in India and the international commitments made.

answer.model_answer_md:
**In situ (on site) conservation** protects species in their natural habitat, so the whole ecosystem and its biodiversity at all levels are conserved. Biodiversity hotspots, regions of very high species richness and endemism, are priorities; 34 exist, covering under 2 percent of land, and three — Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya — cover India’s richest regions. India legally protects biosphere reserves, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. Sacred groves in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghats of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar in Madhya Pradesh protect forests through tradition. Ramsar sites protect internationally important wetlands, and the IUCN Red Data Book identifies threatened species for priority.

**Ex situ (off site) conservation** removes threatened species to special settings: zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks; cryopreservation of gametes; in vitro fertilisation; tissue culture of plants; and seed banks for commercially important plants. Some animals extinct in the wild survive only in zoos.

**International.** At the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro (1992), nations agreed to conserve biodiversity and use it sustainably; at Johannesburg (2002), 190 countries pledged to reduce significantly the rate of biodiversity loss by 2010.

questions.stem_md: A city council member argues that money spent on conserving wild species is wasted because only a few species are useful to people. Evaluate this argument using the narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical reasons for conservation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Narrowly utilitarian.** The claim underestimates direct benefits. People obtain food, firewood, fibre, construction material and industrial products such as tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins and perfumes from wild species. More than 25 percent of drugs sold today come from plants, and 25,000 plant species are used in traditional medicine. Most species have never been examined, so bioprospecting may yet reveal valuable products in species now thought useless.

**Broadly utilitarian.** Many benefits come as services rather than products. The Amazon forest is estimated to produce about 20 percent of the oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere. Bees, bumblebees, birds and bats pollinate crops, a service that would be very costly to replace. Nature also gives aesthetic pleasure. These benefits depend on many species working together, as the rivet popper hypothesis suggests.

**Ethical.** Every species has an intrinsic value, whether or not it is useful to us, and we have a moral duty to pass on our biological legacy to future generations.

**Judgement.** The argument fails on all three grounds: usefulness is often unknown or indirect, and value is not limited to use, so conservation spending is justified.
